content_metadata.description: Analysis of the video 'Flat Earth | Air Density! AWESO', focusing on the depiction of atmospheric refraction on a flat Earth model, through animations and theories presented by Dr. Zach.

qAndA.answer: Some viewers felt that the simulation made the sun appear higher instead of lower during sunset, which is incorrect.
qAndA.question: What specific concern about atmospheric refraction did Dr. Zach address at the beginning of the video?

qAndA.answer: He suggested using a large swimming pool to observe how a light source appears when viewed from far away, demonstrating the combined effects of refraction and perspective.
qAndA.question: What specific proposal did Dr. Zach make for a physical experiment to investigate the theory about the sun's setting?
What software program did Dr. Zach and Steve use to create their flat Earth model simulations?

qAndA.answer: The stars were placed at a fixed altitude of 4,000 miles above the Earth, with accurate angles that match observations from different points on Earth.
qAndA.question: What specific feature of the AutoCAD flat Earth model was highlighted as evidence for the consistency of star trails across locations?

qAndA.answer: The moon was made slightly flattened so that the lunar phases would accurately reflect what is observed in reality.
qAndA.question: What aspect of the moon's appearance in the flat Earth model required a slight modification to its shape?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi, Flat Earthers. This is Zach.
And this is Steve. In the previous video, we gave you an introduction on how the refraction
in the atmosphere, or the atmosphere, was the solution to the various visual problems
that were not working on flat earth models. If you haven't watched that video yet, click
on this link to watch it now.
Today we're going to explain a little bit more by showing you the star trails from different
locations on the flat earth. Many people thought that the video we showed before was not
enough to prove that refraction is the reason why the sun rises and sets. And many others
thoughts that refraction would make the apparent sun appear higher up instead of down.
So to make this clear, let me tell you that what we did was add the atmosphere to the
flat earth model in cinema for D. And cinema for D made the apparent sun go down, not us.
So if there is anything wrong with this, then it will be cinema for D's fault. If you
disagree with the software, please send them an email and see what they will tell you.
Now picture the sun is about you and the last layer of the atmosphere or the atmosphere
plane is a lot closer to you than the sun. The refraction will happen until the last
layer of the atmosphere plane which goes to the ground, right? So looking at the sun from
the ground through the atmosphere plane can make the apparent sun appear lower instead
of higher. And if you look at it this way, the apparent sun will appear higher, right?
But this is all incorrect. What you will see from the ground is the apparent sun only.
So whether it appears here or there, it is always lower and the real sun is always higher.
Now the question is what makes the sun go down as it moves away from you? There are
a few theories about this, but they can all be wrong. But let us explain one theory. If
the atmosphere plane is only 5 miles up and the apparent sun is right above it then yes,
perspective can make the sun go down in less than 7000 miles away from the observer. And
this will make the flat earth model work. But you and I believe that the atmosphere plane
or the atmosphere is a lot thicker than that. Therefore perspective will help a little,
but not a lot.
So if the real sun moves to the west for about 4000 miles, how would the apparent sun look
like from the observer's perspective? We can guess, but we will not know until we make
a physical experiment that represents all of this. For example, we can do this in a big
swimming pool to see how it reflected, but we look like from far away in order to see
both the reflection and perspective in action. If you guys can help, please contact us and
let us prove this scientifically. But for now, we just call it a theory.
Because we are just trying to prove it in a 3D program, I am pretty sure we are correct,
but we just call it a theory. Here is how the real sun and the apparent sun move in cinema
for D. It is acting exactly how we expected. The apparent sun appears to move faster than
the real sun. Therefore, it disappears in less than 7000 miles away from the observer.
When the apparent sun is at 0 degrees, the real sun is at 35 degrees. And as the real
sun rises at its normal speed, the apparent sun follows at a higher speed. The more they
rise, the closer they get. And when they are 90 degrees, the reflection is zero.
This is a diagram I made in AutoCAD with the real elevation angles of the sun that we
get from SoundCalk.org. This is the location and days that I used. You can try that yourself.
So when we draw the angles accurately, we notice that the sun travels faster the more
it moves away from the observer. As you can see, the distance between 5 and 6 pm is a lot
longer than the distance between 4 and 5 pm. And the distance between 12 and 1 pm is very
close to the speed of the sun on the tropic of cancer. On the globe model, you can say
it is the speed of the spinning earth in the tropic of cancer. But of course, the apparent
sun doesn't travel in a straight line like the real sun does. So the distance between
each hour should not be so exaggerated. We can draw it like this. But this is nothing
but a diagram. And by the way, if perspective is the reason why the sun sets on the flat
earth, then the more the sun moves away from us, the slower it should appear to us. Imagine
yourself in the middle of a highway. The cause that passes by you will be moving in their
real speed. But as they move away from you, they look like they are slowing down. But
it doesn't happen with the sun, right? In fact, the sun appears to travel faster than
morning moves away from you. So perspective is definitely not the only reason why the sun
go down. Here is how the star field would look if we remove the atmosphere. The place
is Canary Island, Spain. The lens that I used here has a 122 degree field of view. And
as you can see, the star is never set because they are too high for perspective to make
them rise or set. Their altitude now is about 4,000 miles. This number is fairly accurate
and matches the rise and set times shown in the programs such as Stellarium. Now I am
going to play the same video, but with the atmosphere or atmosphere had it. As you can
see, the video has changed completely and the star trails look exactly like the original
picture. Here is the original taken on March 15, 2015.
Now let's play the two videos side by side so you can see the effect of the atmosphere.
We can do this from any location. They all work the same.
And here is another test in France. Look at it carefully and compare it with the original
and let us know if we are doing anything wrong.
And here is how the sun rises and sets in Salinas, California. We still need to make adjustments
to the height of everything, but the atmosphere already makes them rise and set correctly.
The atmosphere was the key to solving the puzzle.
This is a quick view of the stars in all the cats so you can understand how we drove them
in cinema for the. All the stars you see on the model are 4,000 miles up and the angles
of the stars are accurate and they match modern science. We didn't make them up.
And that excels sheets on the left side of the screen shows all the data that we used.
You can find it in the description.
Here is the south view of the stars on the flat earth with the atoms playing at it.
Now this should be enough for some trolls to see that wherever we are on the flat earth,
the sun and the stars we are rising says. And if they don't look like real life, then
please try to understand that by adjusting the map and the heights of all the objects
in the sky can fix the problem. We still don't know for sure the heights of everything
and we still don't know for sure how the real map looks like. The point is that the atmosphere
or atmosphere playing makes everything in the sky rise and set in cinema for D. If you
think that the atmosphere should make things go up instead of down, then please talk
to cinema for D programmers.
Here is something that we're going to talk about in the next video. When the atmosphere
was added, the first thing that we noticed was that spheres looked oblong when viewed
through the refraction. The only way to overcome this was to make the spheres as flat as possible.
For the moon it could not be perfectly flat or the phases would not work. So the moon
is a very flat sphere or almost flat but not 100%.
Don't forget to subscribe to my channel Steve Dorrance where you will find complete versions
of the clips shown. I will also be doing more videos this week showing views from various
locations. Thanks for watching.
